To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a QCL with a reinjection provided by two external targets in double cavity configuration can be used to realize a displacement sensor with sub-nanometric resolution.

we demonstrated a novel method to measure nanometric displacements by means of a QCL-based system, which is based on the stroboscopic-like behavior of the laser dynamics and on the interferometric signal of two external targets.
a QCL with a double cavity configuration can be used as an ultrasensitive displacement sensor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and characterization of advanced QCL-based sensors.
the study of QCLs as sources for advanced sensors.
the study of the fundamental physics of quantum cascade lasers, with the aim to realize a displacement sensor with a resolution better than 10 nm.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed scheme allows to obtain a displacement sensor with a resolution of about 1nm.

the proposed sensor is based on the exploitation of the intrinsic nonlinear behavior of a QCL in a self-mixing scheme and that, by means of the stroboscopic effect induced by the two targets, the sensor allows for a nanometric resolution of the target displacement, with a bandwidth of 1 kHz.
the system under study is capable of detecting the slow motion of the target with a resolution of the order of 10 nm, which is the limit set by the intrinsic stability of the QCL.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the system exploits the intrinsic nonlineary of QCLs to access the nanometric resolution of a displacement sensor.
the system is able to detect the displacement of one target with a sensitivity that depends on the displacement of the other target.
the system exploits the nonlinear dynamics of QCLs, and the ultra-stability in self-mixinging configuration, to access a displacement sensor with a sensitivity of a few nanometers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the QCL can be used as a nanometric sensor in a self-mixing interferometric setup.
the nonlinear behavior of a QCL can be exploited to access the nanometric regime of motion, even when a single QCL is used as sensor.
the nonlinear dynamics of QCLs can be used to design a displacement sensor with a nanometric resolution and an intrinsic sensitivity to the acceleration of the target.
